newsitem.title: UK: Tin pulled back from peaks, still ends LME higher.
newsitem.headline: Tin pulled back from peaks, still ends LME higher.

text.p: Tin prices came off their highs during late Friday LME trading, responding to the inevitable profit-taking, although the market still ended higher after a session when it, unusually, was the stand-out metal.
Traders said gyrations in the contango, which reflected July date tightness and the usual thinness of the market were responsible for wide price moves.

As some investment funds are perceieved to be long of July, shorts are starting to cover, bringing in the spreads. Cash/threes narrowed in to around $14 at one point before ending at $15/25. At the start of the week this spread was over $50.
This fostered an uptick in prices from midsession, as the market continued to correct up from 14-1/2 month lows hit earlier this week, and last trade was at $5,710, up $40.
Further short-term gains are likely, due to the spread seen remaining under pressure and expectations of some modest stock drawdowns, traders said.
Elsewhere, the action in the markets was generally muted, and there was little significant movement. Copper, for example, was inconclusive under $2,500 and above $2,475.
"Copper has had a dead day - it has been very, very quiet," Martin Squires of LME trader Rudolf Wolff and Co said.
Prices finished at $2,487, up $6, while the cash/threes spread was little different at $57/67.
Aluminium was marooned under $1,600, and spent a featureless session in a narrow range, closing at $1,597, down $3 from Thursday.
Nickel built on earlier steadiness, with some players squaring up their positions ahead of the weekend, and last trade was at $7,310, a $70 gain.
In the short-term the market will remain pre-occupied with the Inco strike at Sudbury, and whether a protracted stoppage will eventually result in stock drawdowns.
Zinc prices fell back into the minus column during the latter part of the session, reacting to profit-taking after the run-up to 4-1/2 year highs earlier, and last trade was at $1,367, down $18.
Lead continued this week's pattern of slow but steady upside progress, and although there was selling near the $650 level last business was still $4 higher at $642.
"The market seem to feel that the downside is limited, so the shorts are taking some profits," Squires said.
The alloy market was quiet, closing at a slightly lower $1,470/75.
